claims.text: Rapid quenching by arc melting on a water-cooled copper hearth increases the coercive field of magnetic high-entropy alloys relative to slower cooling.
Rapid quenching refines the alloy microstructure.
Rapid quenching enhances formation or increases the volume fraction of a C14 Laves phase.
A C14 Laves phase pins magnetic domain walls more effectively than the mixed-phase microstructure produced by slower cooling.
Slower cooling produces a more mixed-phase and coarser microstructure than rapid quenching.
Rapid cooling suppresses diffusional growth of grains and secondary phases.
Rapid cooling produces a finer microstructure with increased defect density.
Fine microstructural features and increased defect density provide effective pinning sites for magnetic domain walls.
Stronger domain-wall pinning increases the coercive field.
The coercivity increase should occur when composition is held constant and cooling rate is the principal processing difference.
The effect is expected only for compositions in which the C14 Laves phase is thermodynamically accessible.
The effect requires rapid quenching that does not introduce detrimental residual stresses.
The magnitude of the coercivity change may depend on alloy composition and heat-treatment parameters in addition to cooling rate.
